Sharp
shahrp
adj.
Old English scearp, cutting, keen. Webster 1828: having a very thin edge or fine point; keen; piercing; also severe, harsh, biting. In the Authorized Version the word belongs overwhelmingly to two things — swords and tongues — and Scripture repeatedly puts them in the same sentence.

Biblical Definition

Sharp in Scripture is a word about edges, and its most sustained use joins the edge of a blade to the edge of speech. Isaiah’s Servant is equipped as a weapon: he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me (Isaiah 49:2). The risen Christ appears with the same figure made literal: out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword (Revelation 1:16). The image is not decorative. It says the Lord’s conquest is accomplished by speech, and that His word is an instrument that cuts. Hebrews makes the claim explicit and turns it on the reader: the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart (Hebrews 4:12). Scripture is not primarily the object of the reader’s examination; it is the instrument of his. But the same edge exists in fallen mouths, and David names it: the wicked are those whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword (Psalm 57:4). Luke even records sharpness among the apostles — the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder (Acts 15:39). The faculty is the same. Only the hand differs.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SHARP as having a very thin edge or fine point; keen; acute; piercing; severe; also, eager, quick of perception, and biting in speech. Webster gives both the physical and the verbal sense under one head.

expand to see more

SHARP, a. [Sax. scearp.] — Having a very thin edge or fine point; keen; acute; not blunt. Piercing; penetrating; as a sharp wind. Severe; harsh; biting; sarcastic; as sharp words. Eager; keen; quick, as of appetite or perception.

Webster runs the blade sense and the speech sense together without apology, exactly as the Authorized Version does. A sharp word and a sharp sword are one metaphor in English because they are one metaphor in Scripture, and the reason is given in Hebrews 4:12: God’s speech actually cuts.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 4:12 — "For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart."

Revelation 1:16 — "And he had in his right hand seven stars: and out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword: and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength."

Isaiah 49:2 — "And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me;"

Psalm 57:4 — "My soul is among lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword."

Acts 15:39 — "And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus;"

Modern Corruption

Sharp is corrupted when the sharpness Scripture assigns to God’s word is claimed for the preacher’s manner — harshness mistaken for faithfulness — and, in the opposite direction, when the edge is filed off the Word itself so that it may no longer wound before it heals.

expand to see more

The first corruption flatters the severe. Hebrews 4:12 says the word of God is sharper than any twoedged sword; it does not say the preacher should be. Men who have confused the two produce a ministry that cuts by temperament rather than by text, and then reads the resulting damage as evidence of faithfulness. Acts 15:39 is the standing rebuke: sharpness between brethren is recorded in Scripture without approval, and it separated Paul from Barnabas. Psalm 57:4 puts a sharp tongue squarely among the weapons of the wicked. The edge belongs to the Word. The minister’s calling is to hold it steadily and get out of its way, and Paul’s own instruction is that the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men.

The second corruption is now more common and does more damage. Preaching that has decided in advance never to wound must blunt the instrument, and a blunt sword does not divide soul and spirit or discern the thoughts and intents of the heart — it merely rests on the surface. Where the whole counsel of God is filtered for what will not offend, the hearer is protected from the only thing that could save him. Scripture assumes the wound is the beginning of the healing; the Spirit uses a cutting word to convict before He uses a binding word to comfort. A ministry that removes the first has not become kinder. It has become useless, and it has quietly asserted an authority over the Word that no man has.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew and Greek behind sharp are ordinary adjectives of keenness, and their theological weight comes from the nouns they modify. In the Authorized Version those nouns are almost always a sword or a mouth.

expand to see more

Hebrew chad — sharp, keen (Isaiah 49:2; Psalm 57:4). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.

Hebrew cherev (H2719) — sword; the noun that sharp most often modifies, and the standing image of both warfare and judgment.

Greek machaira (G3162) — a sword or dagger; the word Paul uses for the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Greek tomoteros — sharper, more cutting; the comparative in Hebrews 4:12, from a root meaning to cut. Untagged in this lexicon.

Usage

"The word of God is sharper than any twoedged sword (Hebrews 4:12) — the edge belongs to the text, not the temperament."

"The Servant’s mouth like a sharp sword (Isaiah 49:2) and Christ’s sharp twoedged sword (Revelation 1:16): the conquest is by speech."

"A sharp tongue sits among the weapons of the wicked (Psalm 57:4), and sharp contention divided Paul from Barnabas (Acts 15:39)."
